Urban Canopy Cover and Heat Exposure

Prof. Marc Los Huertos  •  Pomona College  •  Spring 2026

← Back to Project Index

Background P1 · Descriptive P1 · Visualization P1 · Statistics P2 · Descriptive P2 · Visualization P2 · Statistics Synthesis

Study overview. This analysis examines how urban tree canopy cover affects heat exposure across five urban land-use settings and three socioeconomic groups in the Inland Empire. Two complementary instrument types were deployed: Part I uses 24-hour infield temperature loggers (continuous air temperature) and Part II uses handheld IR thermometers (point-in-time surface temperature). Together they reveal both chronic heat burden and instantaneous thermal conditions.

Background and Research Context

Urban heat islands (UHIs) emerge when impervious surfaces, reduced vegetation, and waste heat from buildings and vehicles elevate temperatures above surrounding rural areas. Tree canopy provides one of the most cost-effective mitigation strategies — shade reduces incoming radiation while transpiration cools surfaces through latent heat flux.

Environmental justice concerns arise because canopy cover is unevenly distributed: wealthier neighborhoods historically receive more urban greening investment. If canopy reduces heat exposure and low-income communities have less canopy, those communities bear a disproportionate thermal burden.

# ── Set paths — update if your CSVs live elsewhere ───────────────────────────
log_path <- "/home/mwl04747/RTricks/A13_Heat_Islands/Data/infield_logger_canopy_urban.csv"
ir_path  <- "/home/mwl04747/RTricks/A13_Heat_Islands/Data/ir_spot_temperature_canopy_urban.csv"

# ── Part I: infield loggers ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
log_raw <- read_csv(log_path, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(
    urban_setting    = factor(urban_setting,    levels = setting_lvl),
    demographic_group = factor(demographic_group, levels = income_lvl)
  )

# ── Part II: IR spot temperatures ────────────────────────────────────────────
ir_raw <- read_csv(ir_path, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(
    urban_setting    = factor(urban_setting,    levels = setting_lvl),
    demographic_group = factor(demographic_group, levels = income_lvl),
    time_of_day = cut(measurement_hour,
                      breaks = c(8, 11, 14, 17),
                      labels = c("Morning (9–11)", "Midday (12–14)",
                                 "Afternoon (15–17)"),
                      include.lowest = TRUE)
  )

cat("Logger dataset:  ", nrow(log_raw), "rows ×", ncol(log_raw), "columns\n")
## Logger dataset:   180 rows × 6 columns
cat("IR spot dataset: ", nrow(ir_raw),  "rows ×", ncol(ir_raw),  "columns\n")
## IR spot dataset:  600 rows × 7 columns

Two research questions guide this analysis:

  1. Does mean 24-hour air temperature differ by urban setting, income group, and canopy cover? (Part I — loggers)
  2. Does instantaneous surface temperature vary by canopy cover, time of day, urban setting, and income group? (Part II — IR spot)
Part I — Dataset 1

Infield Temperature Loggers

Cold-chain food logistics loggers deployed for 24 hours · 180 observations · 5 settings × 3 income groups

1.3 Normality check

set.seed(42)
norm_tbl <- log_raw |>
  group_by(urban_setting) |>
  summarise(
    n  = n(),
    W  = round(shapiro.test(mean_air_temperature_c)$statistic, 4),
    p  = round(shapiro.test(mean_air_temperature_c)$p.value,   4),
    Skew = round(moments::skewness(mean_air_temperature_c), 3),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(Normal = ifelse(p > 0.05, "Yes", "No"))

kable(norm_tbl,
      caption = "Shapiro-Wilk normality test per urban setting (logger data)",
      col.names = c("Setting","N","W","p-value","Skewness","Normal?")) |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Shapiro-Wilk normality test per urban setting (logger data)
Setting N W p-value Skewness Normal?
School 36 0.9578 0.1843 0.239 Yes
Park 36 0.9666 0.3401 0.144 Yes
Commercial 36 0.9695 0.4132 0.310 Yes
Parking Lot 36 0.9567 0.1698 -0.664 Yes
Playground 36 0.9667 0.3427 -0.381 Yes

💡 Why normality matters here One-way ANOVA assumes approximately normal residuals within each group. With n = 36 per setting, the Central Limit Theorem provides reasonable robustness — but we will verify residual normality after fitting and use Kruskal-Wallis as a non-parametric check.

📊 What to look for in these plots If environmental justice patterns are present, you expect: (a) low-income sites cluster at lower canopy cover and higher temperatures, (b) parking lots and commercial areas show the highest temperatures regardless of income group, and (c) the scatter plot shows a negative slope (more canopy → cooler air).

3. Statistical Analysis — Logger Data

3.1 One-way ANOVA: does temperature differ by urban setting?

H₀: Mean 24-hour air temperature is equal across all five urban settings. H₁: At least one setting has a different mean temperature.

aov_setting <- aov(mean_air_temperature_c ~ urban_setting, data = log_raw)
summary(aov_setting)
##                Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)
## urban_setting   4    2.5  0.6173   0.247  0.911
## Residuals     175  436.6  2.4951
tidy(aov_setting) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 4))) |>
  kable(caption = "ANOVA table: air temperature ~ urban setting") |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
ANOVA table: air temperature ~ urban setting
term df sumsq meansq statistic p.value
urban_setting 4 2.4691 0.6173 0.2474 0.9109
Residuals 175 436.6408 2.4951 NA NA

3.2 Post-hoc comparisons (Tukey HSD)

em_setting <- emmeans(aov_setting, ~ urban_setting)
pairs_setting <- pairs(em_setting, adjust = "tukey")
summary(pairs_setting) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 4)),
         sig = case_when(p.value < 0.001 ~ "***",
                         p.value < 0.01  ~ "**",
                         p.value < 0.05  ~ "*",
                         TRUE            ~ "")) |>
  kable(caption = "Tukey HSD pairwise comparisons — urban setting") |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)

3.7 Non-parametric check: Kruskal-Wallis test

kw_setting <- kruskal.test(mean_air_temperature_c ~ urban_setting, data = log_raw)
kw_income  <- kruskal.test(mean_air_temperature_c ~ demographic_group, data = log_raw)

tibble(
  Test      = c("Urban setting", "Income group"),
  Chi_sq    = round(c(kw_setting$statistic, kw_income$statistic), 3),
  df        = c(kw_setting$parameter, kw_income$parameter),
  p_value   = round(c(kw_setting$p.value, kw_income$p.value), 4),
  Sig       = ifelse(c(kw_setting$p.value, kw_income$p.value) < 0.05, "✓", "—")
) |>
  kable(caption = "Kruskal-Wallis tests (non-parametric alternative to ANOVA)") |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Kruskal-Wallis tests (non-parametric alternative to ANOVA)
Test Chi_sq df p_value Sig
Urban setting 1.132 4 0.8892 —
Income group 1.856 2 0.3953 —

📊 Interpreting the logger results A significant ANOVA F-test tells you that at least one setting has a different mean temperature. The Tukey HSD post-hoc narrows down which pairs differ. The regression slope on canopy cover quantifies how much each additional percent of canopy is associated with cooler (or warmer) air. If the income group coefficient is significant in the multiple regression, it suggests that income group predicts temperature even after accounting for canopy and setting — consistent with an environmental justice pattern.

5. Visualization — IR Spot Data

5.1 Surface temperature distributions

p_box2 <- ggplot(ir_raw,
                 aes(x = urban_setting, y = ir_surface_temperature_c,
                     fill = urban_setting)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.2, outlier.size = 0.8, width = 0.55) +
  geom_jitter(aes(color = demographic_group), width = 0.1,
              alpha = 0.25, size = 1) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point",
               shape = 23, size = 2.5, fill = "white", color = "#1e3a2f") +
  scale_fill_manual(values  = setting_pal, guide = "none") +
  scale_color_manual(values = income_pal,  name  = "Income group") +
  labs(title = "IR Surface Temperature by Urban Setting",
       subtitle = "◇ = mean; points colored by income group",
       x = NULL, y = "Surface temperature (°C)") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1))

p_dens2 <- ggplot(ir_raw,
                  aes(x = ir_surface_temperature_c, fill = urban_setting,
                      color = urban_setting)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.25, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 35, linetype = "dashed",

  scale_color_manual(values = setting_pal, name = "Setting") +

6. Statistical Analysis — IR Spot Data

6.1 One-way ANOVA: surface temperature by urban setting

aov2_setting <- aov(ir_surface_temperature_c ~ urban_setting, data = ir_raw)
tidy(aov2_setting) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 4)),
         sig = case_when(p.value < 0.001 ~ "***", p.value < 0.01 ~ "**",
                         p.value < 0.05 ~ "*", TRUE ~ "")) |>
  kable(caption = "ANOVA: IR surface temperature ~ urban setting") |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)

6.4 Kruskal-Wallis: time of day effect

kw_tod <- kruskal.test(ir_surface_temperature_c ~ time_of_day, data = ir_raw)

  Test    = "Time of day (Morning / Midday / Afternoon)",
  Chi_sq  = round(kw_tod$statistic, 3),
  df      = kw_tod$parameter,
  p_value = round(kw_tod$p.value,   4),
  Sig     = ifelse(kw_tod$p.value < 0.05, "✓", "—")
) |>
  kable(caption = "Kruskal-Wallis: does surface temperature vary by time of day?") |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)

6.7 Model comparison: does adding hour improve fit?

lm2_base   <- lm(ir_surface_temperature_c ~
                   canopy_cover_percent + urban_setting + demographic_group,
                 data = ir_raw)
lm2_withhour <- lm2_multi   # already includes measurement_hour

anova(lm2_base, lm2_withhour) |>
  tidy() |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 4))) |>
  kable(caption = "Likelihood ratio test: does measurement hour improve model fit?") |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)

6.8 Interaction: does canopy effect vary by income group?

lm2_interact <- lm(ir_surface_temperature_c ~
                     canopy_cover_percent * demographic_group +
                     measurement_hour + urban_setting,
                   data = ir_raw)

tidy(lm2_interact) |>
  filter(str_detect(term, "canopy|demographic|:")) |>
  mutate(
    sig = case_when(p.value < 0.001 ~ "***", p.value < 0.01 ~ "**",
                    p.value < 0.05  ~ "*",   TRUE ~ ""),
    across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 4))
  ) |>
  kable(caption = "Interaction model: canopy × income group coefficients (selected terms)") |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)

6.9 Residual diagnostics

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
plot(lm2_multi, main = "IR Multiple Regression Diagnostics")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

📊 Key interpretations — IR surface temperature The multiple regression coefficient on canopy_cover_percent gives the average surface temperature reduction (°C) per additional percent of canopy, holding hour, setting, and income constant. A significant interaction between canopy and income group would mean the canopy benefit is distributed unequally — e.g., the cooling effect per percent canopy differs between high- and low-income sites. Compare model AIC to confirm whether adding measurement hour materially improves fit.

Synthesis

# Side-by-side: income group means for both instruments
p_log_inc <- log_raw |>
  group_by(demographic_group) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(mean_air_temperature_c),
            se   = sd(mean_air_temperature_c) / sqrt(n()), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = demographic_group, y = mean, ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se,
             color = demographic_group)) +
  geom_pointrange(size = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = income_pal, guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Logger: air temp by income", x = NULL, y = "Mean temp (°C)") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1))

p_ir_inc <- ir_raw |>
  group_by(demographic_group) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(ir_surface_temperature_c),
            se   = sd(ir_surface_temperature_c) / sqrt(n()), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = demographic_group, y = mean, ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se,
             color = demographic_group)) +
  geom_pointrange(size = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = income_pal, guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "IR spot: surface temp by income", x = NULL, y = "Mean temp (°C)") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1))

p_log_inc + p_ir_inc

# Canopy slopes comparison
p_slope_log <- ggplot(log_raw,
                      aes(x = canopy_cover_percent,
                          y = mean_air_temperature_c,
                          color = demographic_group)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 1.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = income_pal, name = "Income") +
  labs(title = "Logger: canopy vs air temp",
       x = "Canopy (%)", y = "Air temp (°C)")

p_slope_ir <- ggplot(ir_raw,
                     aes(x = canopy_cover_percent,
                         y = ir_surface_temperature_c,
                         color = demographic_group)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 1.2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = income_pal, name = "Income") +
  labs(title = "IR: canopy vs surface temp",
       x = "Canopy (%)", y = "Surface temp (°C)")

p_slope_log + p_slope_ir +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

🔑 Key takeaways

  • Logger data (air temperature) captures the chronic 24-hour thermal burden. ANOVA tests whether urban settings differ in mean air temperature; regression quantifies how much canopy cover predicts that temperature.
  • IR spot data (surface temperature) captures instantaneous peak heat exposure and diurnal dynamics. Surface temperatures are substantially higher than air temperatures and are more sensitive to canopy cover, time of day, and impervious surface type.
  • Environmental justice signal: if low-income sites systematically have lower canopy cover and higher temperatures — and if the income group coefficient remains significant after controlling for canopy and setting — that is evidence of disproportionate heat burden.
  • Canopy effect: a negative coefficient on canopy_cover_percent in both regressions confirms cooling. Compare the coefficient magnitude between the two instruments and across income groups to assess equity in the cooling benefit.
  • Interaction terms: a significant canopy × income interaction means the cooling benefit per percent canopy differs by income group — the most direct test of whether greening investments would have equitable outcomes.
